subject: health
topic: Common Household Cleaning Agents May Cause Subclinical Chronic Respiratory Inflammation
angle: While VOCs are linked to asthma onset, wheezing, and respiratory irritation, experimental data shows they cause dose-related symptoms without significantly changing lung function or biomarkers of airway inflammation.
title: The Hidden Cost of Clean

hooks.text: Does your cleaning routine irritate your lungs?
You feel the irritation, but your lung function remains normal.
You are breathing in dose-related respiratory symptoms every time you clean.
A sharp scent lingers in an empty kitchen.

reveal.headline: Your cleaning products cause symptoms without changing your lung function.
reveal.body: Experimental data shows that volatile organic compounds (VOCs) cause dose-related respiratory symptoms, but they do not significantly change lung function or biomarkers of airway inflammation.

explain.headline: The evidence on VOCs is mixed.
explain.body: Research shows VOCs are linked to asthma onset and wheezing. However, these exposures do not always result in measurable changes to lung function or specific inflammation biomarkers. Results vary by age, country, and individual sensitivity.

matters.headline: Your irritation might be a subclinical response.
matters.body: That may be why you feel a persistent tightness or irritation in your throat and nose. The evidence suggests your body reacts to these chemicals even when standard tests show no damage.

example.headline: The kitchen after a deep clean.
example.body: You finish scrubbing the counters. The sharp scent of bleach and ammonia lingers in the air. You take a breath and feel a slight tickle in your chest.

question.headline: What is in the air you just cleaned?

stat.label: the medium-sized effect size of VOCs on the onset of asthma

claims.text: VOC exposures caused dose-related increases in lower respiratory, upper respiratory, and non-respiratory symptoms, with no significant change in lung function.
claims.quote: VOC exposures caused dose-related increases in lower respiratory, upper respiratory, and non-respiratory symptoms, with no significant change in lung function (FEV(1);, FVC, or FEF(25-75), nasal lavage cellularity or differential cell counts, induced sputum cellularity or differential cell counts, or biomarkers of airway inflammation, including IL-8, LTB(4), or albumin in nasal lavage or induced sputum samples.

claims.text: A meta-analysis suggests that VOCs have a medium-sized effect on the onset of asthma with an effect size of ~0.37.
claims.quote: Our analysis suggests that VOCs have a medium-sized effect on pulmonary diseases, including the onset of asthma (effect size (or Cohen’s d) ~0. 37; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0. 25–0. 49; n = 23)

claims.text: A meta-analysis suggests that VOCs have a medium-sized effect on wheezing with an effect size of ~0.26.
Atopic individuals had significantly reduced FEE(25-75) following exposure to VOCs at 50 mg/m(3).
claims.quote: Atopic individuals had significantly reduced FEE(25-75) following exposure to VOCs at 50 mg/m(3), suggesting that these individuals may be more sensitive to the health effects of VOCs.

claims.text: Prolonged exposure to VOCs has been associated with respiratory irritation, neurological effects, and an increased risk of chronic diseases.

verdict: The evidence confirms that VOCs are associated with respiratory symptoms and asthma onset, but it also shows that these exposures do not necessarily result in measurable changes to lung function or specific inflammation biomarkers.
caveat: The studies show varying results based on country, age, disease type, and individual sensitivity, such as in atopic individuals.
caption:
Common household cleaning agents contain volatile organic compounds that impact your respiratory health.

Research confirms these compounds are linked to asthma onset and wheezing, yet they often cause symptoms without changing measurable lung function. Results vary depending on your age and individual sensitivity.
